RoboBench: A Comprehensive Evaluation Benchmark for Multimodal Large Language Models as Embodied Brain. arXiv:2510.17801.
creator: Yulin Luo, Chun-Kai Fan, Menghang Dong, Jiayu Shi, Mengdi Zhao, Bo-Wen Zhang, Cheng Chi, Jiaming Liu, Gaole Dai, Rongyu Zhang, Ruichuan An, Kun Wu, Zhengping Che, Shaoxuan Xie, Guocai Yao, Zhongxia Zhao, Pengwei Wang, Guang Liu, Zhongyuan Wang, Tiejun Huang, Shanghang Zhang (Peking University, Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence, Fudan University, University of Science and Technology Beijing, Beijing Innovation Center of Humanoid Robotics)
description: RoboBench is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as embodied brains for robotic manipulation. It defines five dimensions—instruction comprehension, perception reasoning, generalized planning, affordance prediction, and failure analysis—spanning 14 capabilities, 25 tasks, and 6092 QA pairs. The benchmark draws from large-scale real robotic data and in-house collection, and introduces an MLLM-as-world-simulator evaluation framework for assessing long-horizon planning feasibility.
name: RoboBench
publisher: Peking University / Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence
rai:annotationsPerItem: Multiple annotations per item via majority-vote strategy; 20 professionally trained annotators conducted comprehensive quality inspections. Specific number of annotations per item not stated beyond the quality control process.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Quality control was performed via a two-stage process: (1) data filtering during construction using general and task-specific filters; (2) post-construction validation by 20 professionally trained annotators checking linguistic clarity, answerability, and correctness. A majority-vote strategy was applied: items all models solve correctly are removed, and items all models fail are manually reviewed and corrected. Human evaluation was also conducted on 438 sampled long-horizon planning tasks to validate the MLLM-as-world-simulator metric, achieving a Pearson correlation of r=0.83 with human judgments (vs. r=0.73 for a baseline LLM scoring approach).
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Custom in-house annotation pipeline using VLMs (Gemini), detection models, and human expert annotators. No third-party crowdsourcing platform (e.g., Mechanical Turk) is mentioned.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotation followed a multi-stage pipeline: (1) preprocessing raw robotic video data; (2) annotation using VLMs (Gemini for video segmentation and structured annotation), detection models, and human experts; (3) Q&A format generation. For planning, Gemini generated structured annotations refined by human annotators. For perception, human annotators labeled bounding boxes and spatial/causal relations. For failure analysis, execution-level failures were labeled by expert annotators. A two-stage quality control process was applied: data filtering during construction (general and task-specific filters) and post-construction validation by 20 professionally trained annotators checking linguistic clarity, answerability, and correctness. A majority-vote strategy was also applied: items all models solve correctly are removed, and items all models fail are manually reviewed.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected from open-source and in-house robotic datasets. For planning, a planning pool was built from high-quality robotic videos from sources including Open X-Embodiment, RH20T, RoboMIND, and others. Instruction comprehension data uses daily-life scenarios with explicit instructions rewritten into implicit forms using LLMs. Perception data combines real robot data with type/view metadata, curated static attributes, GPT-generated functional properties, Gemini-segmented video steps, and human-annotated bounding boxes. Affordance data was sampled from the planning pool and annotated with contact points, motion trajectories, and base positions. Failure analysis data for execution-level failures was collected from RoboMIND and labeled by experts; planning-level failures were synthesized by perturbing correct instructions.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data includes high-quality robotic videos from large-scale real-world robotic datasets (Open X-Embodiment, RH20T, RDT-1B, EmbodiedGPT, RoboMIND, AgiBot World, and others), as well as in-house collected robotic manipulation data. Data spans single-arm, dual-arm, and mobile manipulation embodiments across diverse real-world scenes.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping
rai:dataLimitations: The paper identifies several limitations through experimental findings: (1) existing MLLMs show severe degradation on implicit instructions (average scores dropping ~30%); (2) models struggle with robot-view recognition and temporal grounding; (3) complex planning remains a primary bottleneck, especially for dual-arm coordination and rare-object reasoning; (4) multi-view inputs yield only modest gains and do not close the gap to human performance; (5) execution-level failure diagnosis is extremely challenging even for humans (human score 47.30 vs. 80.67 on planning error). The benchmark focuses on manipulation tasks and may not cover all aspects of embodied intelligence.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Post-collection manipulations include: (1) rewriting explicit instructions into implicit forms using LLMs to create paired explicit-implicit instruction data; (2) synthesizing planning-level failure data by perturbing correct instructions (wrong object, missing step, wrong order); (3) mapping natural language step descriptions to predefined function templates; (4) instantiating function arguments with specific object references; (5) applying majority-vote filtering to remove items all models solve correctly or flagging items all models fail for manual review.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Data preprocessing includes: (1) extracting frame sequences from robotic videos as standardized inputs; (2) using Gemini to generate structured annotations including task summaries, step-wise instructions with timestamps, and metadata (objects, actions, scenes, embodiments); (3) refining annotations by human annotators; (4) mapping steps into function templates (e.g., pick_up(object), move_to(object, target)); (5) standardizing all perception data into multiple-choice QA format; (6) applying general and task-specific filters for image quality and task validity (e.g., excluding single-arm data from dual-arm tasks).
rai:dataSocialImpact: RoboBench provides a unified scaffold for measuring embodied cognition and guiding the development of more robust, generalizable embodied intelligence. By systematically evaluating MLLMs as embodied brains, it aims to advance robotic intelligence for manipulation in dynamic, unstructured environments, which has broad implications for robotics applications in real-world settings. The benchmark exposes fundamental limitations of current MLLMs, helping direct research toward more capable and reliable robotic systems.
rai:dataUseCases: RoboBench is intended for: (1) systematic evaluation of MLLMs as embodied brains for robotic manipulation; (2) benchmarking high-level cognitive capabilities including instruction comprehension, perception reasoning, generalized planning, affordance prediction, and failure analysis; (3) establishing a leaderboard for state-of-the-art MLLMs; (4) providing actionable insights for advancing embodied brain development in robotic AI; (5) guiding development of next-generation MLLMs toward more robust robotic intelligence.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Gemini (used for video segmentation, generating structured annotations including task summaries, step-wise instructions with timestamps, and metadata); GPT (used for generating functional properties and distractors for object-centric perception data, and for rewriting explicit instructions into implicit forms using LLMs); detection models (used in the annotation pipeline for perception tasks).
